title: Vercel Sandbox Alternatives for AI Agents and Code Execution
summary: Compare Vercel Sandbox alternatives on isolation, memory-preserving pause, GPUs, session limits and hourly cost, with rates for E2B, Daytona, Modal and Beam.
body_markdown:
The main Vercel Sandbox alternatives are E2B, Daytona, Modal, Cloudflare's sandboxes and Beam. Which one fits depends on what Vercel Sandbox doesn't give you. For a pause that keeps running processes, look at E2B, a Daytona VM sandbox or a Beam VM. For GPUs, look at Modal, Daytona or a Beam sandbox. If your backend already runs on Workers, Cloudflare is the natural pick. This guide compares them on isolation, state, session limits and hourly cost.


## What Vercel Sandbox does well, and where it stops


Vercel Sandbox runs each sandbox in its own Firecracker microVM with a dedicated kernel, bills CPU only while code is using it, and saves the filesystem automatically when a sandbox stops. It is a good default for an app that already deploys on Vercel. The reasons to look elsewhere are processes that don't survive a stop, no GPU option, fixed sandbox shapes and a setup tied to a Vercel project.


What it does well:


- **MicroVM isolation.** Every sandbox gets its own kernel, which is the stronger boundary for code you didn't write. Our[microVM explainer](https://www.beam.cloud/blog/what-is-a-microvm) covers why that matters.
- **Persistent by default.** When a session stops, Vercel snapshots the filesystem, and the next SDK call on that sandbox resumes from the snapshot.
- **Active CPU billing.** CPU is metered only while your code uses it, so time spent waiting on a model call or a network request isn't billed as CPU.
- **High limits on Pro.** A Pro team can run 10,000 sandboxes at once, in 19 regions.
- **Two SDKs and a CLI.** There are SDKs for JavaScript and TypeScript and for Python 3.11 or newer.


Where it stops:


- **A stop keeps files, not processes.** A session is one boot of the microVM. Resuming a sandbox starts a new session from the last filesystem snapshot, so a dev server, a REPL or an agent that was mid-task has to be started again. Vercel's` onResume` hook exists for that restart.
- **Sessions end.** The default timeout is 5 minutes. One session can run for at most 45 minutes on Hobby and 24 hours on Pro and Enterprise.
- **No GPUs.** The resource limits cover vCPUs and memory, and the docs list no GPU option.
- **Fixed shapes.** Each vCPU comes with 2 GB of memory. The largest sandbox is 4 vCPUs and 8 GB on Hobby, 8 vCPUs and 16 GB on Pro, and 32 vCPUs and 64 GB on Enterprise.
- **Memory and snapshots are billed while idle.** Provisioned memory is charged for the whole session, including time the CPU sits idle, and automatic snapshots count toward snapshot storage.
- **It lives inside a Vercel project.** The SDK authenticates with a Vercel OIDC token, or with an access token plus a team ID and a project ID. Custom images are pulled from Vercel Container Registry, and a custom image's` ENTRYPOINT` and` CMD` don't run.


## Vercel Sandbox alternatives compared


E2B and Daytona are the closest matches for agent code execution, Modal and Beam add GPUs, and Cloudflare suits teams whose backend is a Worker. The table shows how each one isolates code, what it keeps when a sandbox stops, whether it offers GPUs and how long one session can run.


Option Isolation What a stop or pause keeps GPUs Longest session SDKs


Vercel Sandbox Firecracker microVM Files, through an automatic snapshot No 24 hours on Pro, 45 minutes on Hobby JavaScript and TypeScript, Python


E2B Firecracker microVM Files and memory on pause No 24 hours on Pro, 1 hour on Hobby JavaScript and TypeScript, Python


Daytona Container by default; Linux VM sandboxes Files; VM sandboxes pause with memory Yes 15-minute idle auto-stop by default, can be disabled Python, TypeScript, Ruby, Go, Java


Modal Sandboxes gVisor or a VM runtime Files through snapshots; memory snapshots in alpha Yes, on the gVisor runtime 24 hours Python, JavaScript, Go


Cloudflare sandboxes MicroVM per container instance Files through snapshots No GPU instance types listed Until the inactivity timeout, 6 hours at most TypeScript, from a Worker


Beam sandbox Container by default; microVM with use_vm=True Filesystem images and memory snapshots Yes Set by its lifetime; -1 removes the limit Python, TypeScript


Beam VM MicroVM Files on stop; memory and processes on pause No Runs until you stop it CLI, Python, JavaScript


A few notes on reading it. "Longest session" is one continuous run. A Vercel sandbox and a paused E2B sandbox can both be resumed again and again, so the cap applies to each stretch of work. On Cloudflare, a sandbox is a container started by a Durable Object in your Worker; code running inside it doesn't count as activity, so a long build needs an alarm or open connection to keep the instance alive. Modal's memory snapshots expire 7 days after creation, and its filesystem snapshots after 30 days unless you change the TTL.


## What a sandbox costs per hour on each platform


One hour of a 2 vCPU, 4 GB sandbox runs from $0.044 to $0.34 at list rates, and the spread comes from how each platform meters CPU. Vercel, Modal and Cloudflare bill CPU on use, so an agent that mostly waits on a model costs far less than one compiling code. E2B, Daytona and Beam bill the size you provision for as long as the sandbox runs.


Option Inputs for 2 vCPU and 4 GB One hour, CPU busy One hour, CPU at 10%


Vercel Sandbox, Pro, iad1 $0.128 per active vCPU-hour, $0.0212 per GB-hour provisioned $0.3408 $0.1104


E2B $0.0504 per vCPU-hour, $0.0162 per GiB-hour, both provisioned $0.1656 $0.1656


Daytona $0.0504 per vCPU-hour, $0.0162 per GiB-hour, both provisioned $0.1656 $0.1656


Modal Sandboxes $0.00003942 per physical core-second (one core is 2 vCPUs), $0.00000667 per GiB-second, on the higher of request and use, with a 0.125-core minimum $0.2380 $0.1138 with no CPU requested and 4 GiB in use


Cloudflare, custom instance type 2 vCPUs, 4 GiB, 16 GB disk: $0.000020 per active vCPU-second, $0.0000025 per GiB-second, $0.00000007 per GB-second of disk $0.1840 $0.0544


Beam sandbox, Shared tier $0.011 per vCPU-hour, $0.0055 per GiB-hour, both provisioned $0.0440 $0.0440


Beam sandbox, Performance tier $0.05 per vCPU-hour, $0.01 per GiB-hour, both provisioned $0.1400 $0.1400


The 10% column follows Vercel's own pricing examples, which assume a sandbox spends most of its time waiting on LLM calls. Modal's 10% figure applies when the sandbox requests no CPU: 10% of 2 vCPUs is 0.1 physical cores, which is under Modal's 0.125-core minimum, so the minimum is what gets billed (0.125 × 3,600 × $0.00003942 = $0.0177, plus $0.0960 for memory). A sandbox that requests 2 vCPUs is billed for them at any load, which is $0.2380 an hour. Cloudflare has no predefined 2 vCPU, 4 GiB type, so the row prices a custom instance type with a 16 GB disk, the disk size of the 2 vCPU standard-3 preset, which has 8 GiB of memory. Cloudflare's default account limit is 4 vCPUs and 12 GiB per instance, and it can be raised on request. Beam's Shared tier covers sandboxes up to 8 vCPUs and 16 GiB; new accounts default to Performance, and a sandbox opts in with` cpu_tier="shared"` .


The hourly rate isn't the whole bill:


- **Plan fees.** Vercel Pro usage draws on a $20 monthly credit before it is billed. E2B Pro is $150 a month plus usage. Cloudflare sandboxes need the $5 a month Workers Paid plan, which includes 375 vCPU-minutes and 25 GiB-hours, and Workers and Durable Objects usage is billed alongside the container. Beam's Developer plan is $20 a month and includes $20 of usage credits.
- **Free allowances.** Vercel Hobby includes 5 hours of Active CPU, 420 GB-hours of memory and 5,000 sandbox creations a month. E2B's Hobby plan is free and comes with a one-time $100 usage credit. Daytona includes $200 of free compute.
- **Storage.** Vercel bills snapshot storage at $0.08 per GB-month and sandbox creations at $0.60 per million. E2B includes sandbox disk in the plan. Daytona bills $0.000108 per GiB-hour after the first 5 GiB. Cloudflare's snapshots are free during their public beta. Beam doesn't bill storage yet; the planned rate is $0.0001 per GB-hour of data stored.


Our[E2B pricing](https://www.beam.cloud/blog/e2b-pricing-explained) ,[Daytona pricing](https://www.beam.cloud/blog/daytona-pricing-explained) and[Modal pricing](https://www.beam.cloud/blog/modal-pricing-explained) guides work through larger workloads on those three.


## Vercel Sandbox vs E2B


E2B and Vercel Sandbox both run Firecracker microVMs with a 24-hour session on their paid plans, and neither offers GPUs. They differ in what a pause keeps and in how they bill. E2B's pause saves the filesystem and the memory, so running processes and loaded variables are still there on resume, and a paused sandbox is kept until you delete it. A stopped Vercel sandbox resumes from its files only.


On billing, E2B charges for the vCPUs and memory you provision for every second the sandbox runs, at $0.0504 per vCPU-hour and $0.0162 per GiB-hour. Vercel charges $0.128 per vCPU-hour only while the CPU is active, plus $0.0212 per GB-hour of provisioned memory. For the 2 vCPU, 4 GB sandbox above, that is $0.1656 an hour on E2B at any load, against $0.1104 on Vercel at 10% CPU and $0.3408 with the CPU busy.


The plans differ too. E2B Pro costs $150 a month and allows 100 concurrent sandboxes, with paid add-ons up to 1,100. Vercel Pro allows 10,000. E2B sandboxes top out at 8 vCPUs and 8 GiB of memory, and Vercel Pro's at 8 vCPUs and 16 GB. If E2B is on your shortlist, our[E2B alternatives](https://www.beam.cloud/blog/best-e2b-alternatives) guide compares it with more options.


## Alternatives with GPUs and a Python SDK


Modal, Daytona and Beam can attach a GPU to a sandbox, which Vercel Sandbox and E2B can't. That matters when the agent's code is the GPU workload: running a generated training script, evaluating a model, or rendering.


A[Beam sandbox](https://www.beam.cloud/sandbox) is a disposable environment you drive from Python or TypeScript. It runs in a container by default, and` use_vm=True` runs it in a microVM instead. This one runs on the Shared CPU tier, installs a package into the image, runs code and saves the filesystem as a reusable image:


python


```text
from   beam  import   Image, Sandbox


sb = Sandbox(
cpu= 2  ,
memory= "4Gi"  ,
cpu_tier= "shared"  ,
image=Image(python_version= "python3.11"  ).add_python_packages([ "pandas"  ]),
keep_warm_seconds= 1800  ,
).create()


try  :
result = sb.process.run_code( "import pandas as pd; print(pd.__version__)"  )
print  (result.stdout)


# Save the filesystem; Image.from_id(image_id) boots new sandboxes from it
image_id = sb.create_image_from_filesystem()
finally  :
sb.terminate()
```


The` cpu_tier` argument needs beam-client 0.2.236 or later.` keep_warm_seconds` is the sandbox's lifetime, not an idle timer, so 1800 ends it after 30 minutes unless you call` update_ttl()` . To use a GPU, pass` gpu` with a model name such as` "RTX4090"` and put your CUDA libraries in the image. A GPU sandbox bills the GPU rate plus GPU-attached CPU and memory: $0.69 an hour for an RTX 4090, $0.18972 per vCPU-hour and $0.0198 per GiB-hour. With 2 vCPUs and 4 GiB that is $0.69 + $0.3794 + $0.0792, or about $1.15 an hour. Daytona lists an RTX 4090 at $0.57 an hour preemptible and $0.99 an hour on demand; if vCPU and memory are billed on top at its sandbox rates, 2 vCPUs and 4 GiB add $0.1656 an hour. On supported runtimes a sandbox can also take a memory snapshot with` snapshot_memory()` , which captures process state as well as files, and new sandboxes start from that point. Our guide to[sandboxing AI-generated code](https://www.beam.cloud/blog/sandbox-ai-generated-code) covers timeouts and network rules.


Modal runs GPU sandboxes on its gVisor runtime, and its VM runtime is for workloads that expect a full Linux environment, such as Docker. Modal has SDKs for Python, JavaScript and Go. The[Modal Sandbox alternatives](https://www.beam.cloud/blog/modal-sandbox-alternatives) guide has the details. Daytona offers GPU sandboxes with a choice of GPU type and SDKs in five languages; see our[Daytona alternatives](https://www.beam.cloud/blog/daytona-alternatives) guide.


## Alternatives that keep an agent's processes between sessions


Three of these options can pause a sandbox with its memory, so a test server or a half-finished build is still running when the agent comes back: E2B, Daytona's Linux VM sandboxes and Beam VMs. Vercel Sandbox and Cloudflare keep files across a stop and start processes again.


- **E2B** saves filesystem and memory on` pause()` and restores both on` connect()` . A filesystem-only mode is available when you want a lighter snapshot.
- **Daytona** runs sandboxes as containers by default. Its Linux VM sandboxes add fork, pause and resume, and memory snapshots.
- **A[Beam VM](https://www.beam.cloud/virtual-machines)** is a named Linux machine with a persistent root disk. Pausing keeps memory and processes and stops compute billing; stopping keeps the disk only. VMs are CPU-only.


For a VM that sleeps when nobody is connected and wakes on the next connection:


sh


```text
beam vm new agent-box --cpu-tier shared --cpu 2 --memory 4096
beam vm update agent-box --ttl 300 --idle-action pause --auto-resume
```


The idle timer counts connections such as SSH sessions and SDK calls, not commands running inside the VM, so leave it unset while an agent works unattended.


## How to choose a Vercel Sandbox alternative


Start from the limit you ran into, because each alternative fixes a different one.


- **Your app is on Vercel and sessions are short:** stay on Vercel Sandbox. OIDC auth, Active CPU billing and automatic filesystem snapshots come built in.
- **The agent's processes must survive a pause:** E2B, a Daytona Linux VM sandbox or a Beam VM.
- **The code needs a GPU:** a Beam sandbox, Modal or Daytona.
- **Your backend is a Cloudflare Worker:** Cloudflare's sandboxes, which your Worker starts and reaches by name.
- **You want one account for sandboxes, persistent VMs and GPU endpoints:** Beam.
- **You want to run the platform yourself:** Beam's runtime is open source and can manage instances in your own AWS or GCP account, and E2B and Daytona publish their infrastructure code.


## FAQ


### What is the best alternative to Vercel Sandbox?


It depends on what you need that Vercel Sandbox lacks. E2B is the closest like-for-like option and adds a pause that keeps memory. Modal, Daytona and Beam add GPUs, and Cloudflare fits teams already building on Workers.


### Does Vercel Sandbox have a session limit?


Yes. A session runs for 5 minutes by default, and the maximum is 45 minutes on Hobby and 24 hours on Pro and Enterprise. The cap applies to each session, so a persistent sandbox can be resumed for another session from its last filesystem snapshot.


### How much does Vercel Sandbox cost?


On Pro in the default region it costs $0.128 per hour of Active CPU and $0.0212 per GB-hour of provisioned memory, plus $0.60 per million sandbox creations and $0.08 per GB-month of snapshot storage. A 2 vCPU, 4 GB sandbox costs $0.1104 an hour at 10% CPU and $0.3408 an hour with both vCPUs busy.


### Does Vercel Sandbox support GPUs?


No. Its resource limits cover vCPUs and memory, up to 8 vCPUs and 16 GB on Pro and 32 vCPUs and 64 GB on Enterprise. For GPU work in a sandbox, use Modal, Daytona or Beam.


### Is there a free Vercel Sandbox alternative?


Several have free allowances. E2B's Hobby plan has no monthly fee and comes with a one-time $100 in usage credits, and Daytona includes $200 of free compute. Vercel's own Hobby plan includes 5 hours of Active CPU and 420 GB-hours of memory a month.


### Is E2B or Vercel Sandbox better for AI agents?


Both isolate agent code in Firecracker microVMs. E2B keeps memory and running processes across a pause and bills provisioned CPU, while Vercel Sandbox keeps files only and bills CPU when it is active. E2B fits agents that hold state in running processes, and Vercel fits short, bursty tasks from an app on Vercel.


### Can I use a different sandbox from a Next.js app on Vercel?


Yes. Each alternative is an API you call from server-side code, so a route handler or server action can create a sandbox on E2B, Daytona, Modal or Beam with that provider's SDK and an API key. Beam's TypeScript SDK is the` @beamcloud/beam-js` package.


## Run agent code on Beam


A Beam sandbox gives agent code an isolated environment with optional GPUs, filesystem and memory snapshots, and per-millisecond billing, and a Beam VM keeps a long-lived agent's memory and processes between sessions.[Create a Beam account](https://platform.beam.cloud/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=vercel-sandbox-alternatives) to run the snippet above. Current rates are on the[Beam pricing page](https://www.beam.cloud/pricing) .
